### Section 3: Mindset & Emotional Mastery

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
I f you want to create lasting transformation as a coach, this is where the real work begins.
As coaches, we are not just helping clients set goals or take action—we’re guiding them through the terrain of their inner world. This is where breakthroughs happen. Because without rewiring the limiting beliefs, emotional patterns, and subconscious narratives that shape behavior, surface-level change rarely sticks.
This section equips you to be the kind of coach who goes deeper.
These tools are more than worksheets—they are keys to unlocking identity shifts, emotional healing, and inner alignment. You’ll help your clients:
Bring awareness to unconscious beliefs that sabotage growth
Reframe stories rooted in fear, shame, or powerlessness
Navigate emotional triggers with clarity and self-compassion
Build a mindset that supports long-term success and self-trust
But just as importantly, you’ll elevate your presence as a coach. Using these tools well requires emotional intelligence, attunement, and the courage to hold space when your client is in their most vulnerable moments.
So as you use this section, ask yourself:
“Am I willing to challenge the stories my client is clinging to?”
“Can I guide them through resistance with empathy and strength?”
“Am I modeling the very mindset I want them to embody?”
Because great coaches don’t just help clients feel better—they help them become stronger, more empowered versions of themselves.
This section will help you become that kind of coach.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #10: Rewiring Limiting Belief s

? ? Purpose
This tool is a deep-dive process designed to help clients identify, deconstruct, and replace limiting beliefs that keep them stuck. Unlike simple affirmations, this tool engages the brain’s natural patterning systems — turning mindset work into a real, neurological shift.
It moves your client beyond surface-level awareness and into long-term belief transformation.
When to Use It
After a client identifies a recurring block or self-sabotaging behavior
When motivation, confidence, or follow-through is consistently low
As part of a mindset or identity shift module in your coaching program
To revisit old beliefs that may be resurfacing in a new form
How to Facilitate It
Guide your client through the belief shift using five steps:
Uncover the belief
Explore its origin
Challenge its validity
Rewrite the belief
Reinforce the new belief
Sample Script:
“Let’s walk through this step by step. First, we’ll name the belief. Then we’ll look at where it came from, why it’s stuck around, and most importantly — what you’d like to believe instead.”
Encourage honesty over positivity. The goal is not to slap on a happy thought — it’s to shift the foundation.
? ? What to Watch For
Beliefs that seem factual (e.g., “I’m just not good at business”) — challenge these with evidence and alternative truths
Clients who intellectualize but don’t feel the shift — pause and deepen the emotional connection
Resistance to letting go — ask, “What has this belief protected you from?”
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What belief is keeping you from taking the next step?”
“When did you first start thinking that?”
“If you didn’t believe this, how would you show up differently?”
“What belief would support the person you’re becoming?”
? ? Pro Tips
Use visualization or somatic work to help embed the new belief
Encourage repetition — rewriting beliefs takes time and neural reinforcement
Pair this tool with habit tracking or mindset journaling
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Belief identification prompts
Root cause discovery worksheet
Truth-testing framework
Belief reframe builder
Daily reinforcement plan
Coach Mindset
Beliefs drive behavior. And behavior drives results.
When you help a client rewire just one limiting belief, you open the door to dozens of new possibilities. Don’t rush this process — it’s one of the most transformational gifts you can offer as a coach.
Rewiring Limiting Belief s
We are often unaware of our limiting beliefs because they were “passed down” to us by the attitudes and beliefs of others. As long as they remain unconscious (we are not aware of them) they can hold us back from achieving our fullest potential and experiencing joy. For example, if we have heard all of our life that money is the root of evil then we may unconsciously create situations that limit our financial success out of fear of that evil.
Below is a list of some common “phrases” that we are often told growing up or hear in our community. They are so “normal” that we rarely question their validity or consider how they affect our belief systems or make us unhappy. Of course, there is some truth and a good intention behind most of them, but consider which ones you have been conditioned to believe and how they have impacted your beliefs and your life.
“Money is the root of all evil.”
Good intention: money does not bring happiness and can corrupt
Conditioned fear: negative association with having money; it turns you into a bad person Potential limits: unconsciously avoiding or sabotaging financial success to avoid the “negative qualities” you believe you’ll develop if you have money
“Finish your plate. There are starving people in the world.”
Good intention: don’t be wasteful with food and have compassion for others Conditioned fear: food scarcity or guilt for having more opportunity than others Potential limits: overeating and health problems or holding yourself back to avoid feeling guilty over having more opportunity than others
“Money doesn’t grow on trees.”
Good intention: be intelligent with how you spend your money
Conditioned fear: money scarcity; feeling that there is not enough and it is hard to get Potential limits: not believing you can have what you want if it involves having money and therefore not going for it
Which of these phrases were you conditioned to believe?

Changing Your Perspective by Changing our WORDS !
Perspective is everything when it comes to how we feel, and the words that we use are critical factors of our perspective. Below are some examples of key words that, if changed, will drastically impact our unconscious minds. The shift may seem small, but it can have a drastic effect on our happiness and our overall motivation.
Have To vs Get To:
What areas in your life do you feel and say “I have to”? For example: “I have to go to work.” Change it to “I get to go to work,” and see how different you feel. Now, change YOUR “have to’s” into “get to’s” and try your new perspective on size.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #11: Changing Belief s

? ? Purpose
This tool supports the ongoing transformation of a client’s belief system. While “Rewiring Limiting Beliefs” is deep and structured, this tool is ideal for daily mindset shifts and coaching conversations. It helps clients move from disempowering self-talk to empowering self-concept — with clarity, simplicity, and repeatable practice.
Think of it as belief coaching made practical and actionable.
When to Use It
During a session when a disempowering belief surfaces
As a weekly reflection or journaling exercise
When reinforcing a belief shift from prior mindset work
For clients who need small, consistent shifts vs. deep emotional processing
How to Facilitate It
Walk your client through a clear, five-part shift:
Identify the Belief – “What belief is limiting me?”
Recognize the Pattern – “How does it show up in my life?”
Challenge the Belief – “Is this always true?”
Reframe It – “What belief would empower me more?”
Choose Action – “What’s one step I can take from this new belief?”
Sample Script:
“Let’s take that thought you just said and work with it. Not to judge it — but to understand it, then shift it. Because beliefs aren’t fixed; they’re chosen. Let’s help you choose differently.”
? ? What to Watch For
Vague beliefs — ask for specifics (e.g., “I’m not enough” → “Enough for what?”)
Surface-level reframes — push for honesty and believability
Clients defaulting to old patterns — normalize it, and coach for integration
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What does this belief cost you — emotionally, mentally, or in your actions?”
“When you act from this belief, what choices do you make?”
“Can you think of any evidence that contradicts this belief?”
“What would the version of you who holds the new belief do differently today?”
? ? Pro Tips
Use this tool in group settings or email follow-ups for ongoing belief support
Invite clients to track their belief shifts in a journal or voice note
Encourage practice: Repetition rewires the brain faster than intention alone
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Guided belief shift worksheet
Five-part belief reframe flow
Reflective journaling prompts
Progress tracker or date-stamped affirmations
Coach Mindset
A belief doesn’t need to be loud to be powerful.
Sometimes, a quiet shift — from “I can’t” to “I’m learning how” — is all it takes to unlock momentum. This tool helps clients build those micro-shifts that lead to massive identity transformation over time.
Changing Beliefs
The Table Leg Method
Imagine your belief is like a table top and the evidence that supports your belief is like the table legs. Just like with a table, if you knock enough legs out from under it the belief will collapse.
Then, after you collapse the old, unwanted belief that makes you doubt yourself or your dream, you can use the same method to build up a new one. That’s right, it works in reverse! If you determine a belief that is more empowering that you’d prefer, you can find evidence that SUPPORTS your new belief. Add at least 3 legs and the table will stand.

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Dismantling the OLD belief :
For each belief, what examples in your life or the lives of others can you use to disprove the beliefs you do not want? (Write at least 3 pieces of evidence that EACH belief is either false or possibly not true, essentially knocking legs out from the table of your belief.)

#### ? ? ️ Tool #12: Reframing Negative Experiences

? ? Purpose
This tool helps clients shift their relationship with past experiences that may be holding them back. Instead of avoiding or minimizing pain, this reframing process teaches clients to extract meaning, growth, and power from what once felt like failure or trauma.
Reframing doesn’t erase the past — it rewrites its influence.
When to Use It
When a client is stuck in a story about the past
After identifying a recurring pattern rooted in a painful experience
To turn self-judgment into self-compassion
During breakthrough sessions that require emotional integration
How to Facilitate It
Begin by creating safety and permission to explore the story. Help the client describe the experience without judgment, then guide them through a structured reframe process.
Sample Script:
“Let’s look at this moment not as something that defines you, but as something that has shaped you. The goal isn’t to pretend it was positive — but to ask, ‘What did I learn? Who did I become?’”
Lead them through:
Describe the event
Identify emotions and meaning made at the time
Explore new perspectives
Redefine the narrative
Anchor a new lesson, strength, or identity
? ? What to Watch For
Minimization or avoidance — gently invite honesty while creating emotional safety
Reframing too quickly — validate the pain before moving toward growth
Blame or shame loops — help shift from “what happened to me” to “what’s growing through me”
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What did this experience lead you to believe about yourself?”
“What strengths or skills did you develop because of it?”
“What would you say to your younger self now, knowing what you know?”
“What meaning do you want to choose moving forward?”
? ? Pro Tips
Pair with somatic or expressive techniques (breathwork, journaling, art) for deeper integration
Avoid clichés — powerful reframes are personal and specific
Use this tool to support forgiveness, inner child healing, or identity work
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Event deconstruction worksheet
Thought-emotion-belief mapping
Narrative shift and strength anchor sections
Space to write a new story or self-statement
Coach Mindset
Your client’s story is powerful — but it’s not permanent. As a coach, you’re not rewriting history… you’re helping them re-author their identity. When they shift how they see their past, they unlock freedom in their future.
Reframe Negative Experience s
Identify something that happened that made you frustrated, sad, angry, or disappointed: Ask yourself the following questions:
“What else might be going on here?”
“What did I learn from this experience?”
“What can I do differently next time?”
“What positive outcome eventually came as a result of this situation?”
“What meaning does it have? What purpose does it give me?”
“How can I use this for GOOD?”
Practice: Make a list of any experiences from your past that were “negative” and then identify the positive outcomes and/or the empowering lessons you can take from them.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #13: Developing an Empowered Mindse t

? ? Purpose
This tool helps your client shift from self-doubt and limitation into empowerment and possibility. It brings awareness to how their current mindset affects their choices and results — and gives them the opportunity to choose new beliefs, patterns, and inner narratives.
Empowerment doesn’t come from a motivational quote — it comes from intentionally retraining how we think, speak, and show up. This tool starts that process.
When to Use It
After identifying goals or obstacles
When clients feel stuck, insecure, or afraid to act
As part of mindset work in any coaching niche
Anytime a belief, identity, or inner critic needs to shift
How to Facilitate It
Start by exploring what’s currently fueling the client’s thinking. Then guide them toward consciously reframing their beliefs and self-talk.
Sample Script:
“The way you think creates the way you act. Let’s look at the patterns that may have helped you survive — but are no longer helping you thrive. From there, we’ll rewrite the story you want to live from.”
Break it into three layers:
Awareness – What do I currently believe and how is it showing up?
Challenge – Is this belief true? Helpful? Empowering?
Reframe – What mindset would serve my goals and values better?
? ? What to Watch For
Clients struggling to identify limiting beliefs – help them name what they say to themselves under stress
Resistance to reframing – validate the old belief before rewriting it
“Toxic positivity” – reframe in a way that feels honest and grounded, not forced
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“When you think about [goal], what thoughts immediately come up?”
“Whose voice is that? Is it yours, or something you learned?”
“What belief would feel more empowering and believable to you right now?”
“How would someone who already believed that behave this week?”
? ? Pro Tips
Link this tool with others like “Rewiring Limiting Beliefs” and “Changing Beliefs”
Encourage clients to post reframed affirmations where they’ll see them often
Return to this process regularly — mindset shifts are layered and nonlinear
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Mindset self-assessment prompts
Space to uncover and reframe limiting beliefs
Positive affirmations aligned with goals and values
Journaling sections for pattern tracking and reflection
Coach Mindset
Mindset is the soil where all other growth takes root. If your client’s beliefs are misaligned with their goals, no strategy will stick. This tool is how you plant new beliefs — and help your client nurture them into action.
Developing an Empowered Mindse t
Make a list of positive or empowering words you find yourself saying to yourself or using on a weekly basis that you think could trigger positive mindset?
EMPOWERING WORDS:
Write down any positive or empowering conversations you find yourself having with yourself or having with others in a weekly basis?

What positive or empowering expectations and beliefs do you have in these areas:

#### ? ? ️ Tool #14: Unworthiness and Succes s

? ? Purpose
This tool helps clients uncover and shift deep-rooted beliefs that equate success with unworthiness, guilt, or fear. Many high-potential clients unconsciously sabotage opportunities or play small because they don’t feel they deserve more — more money, freedom, visibility, or joy.
This tool brings those patterns to light, helps clients separate their identity from their conditioning, and step into a version of success that feels safe, aligned, and earned from within.
When to Use It
When clients feel uncomfortable receiving success or praise
If they sabotage momentum once things start going well
During visibility, income, or leadership growth phases
When past wounds or imposter syndrome are blocking progress
How to Facilitate It
Begin by helping your client recognize where their sense of unworthiness is rooted — family dynamics, early failure, shame, or cultural messaging. Then guide them to redefine success on their own terms and build new emotional “safety” around it.
Sample Script:
“Success isn’t something you have to earn by being perfect — it’s something you allow when you believe you’re enough. Let’s uncover what’s standing in the way of you fully receiving what you’ve worked for.”
Walk through:
Explore their current definition of success
Identify any beliefs that create conflict (e.g., “If I succeed, I’ll lose people,” “I don’t deserve this”)
Trace back the origin of those beliefs
Redefine success in values-based, self-honoring terms
Create emotional safety around success using visualization, boundaries, and mindset rituals
? ? What to Watch For
Clients who deflect compliments or downplay wins
Avoidance of visibility or expansion — may signal fear of outgrowing others
Perfectionism and overwork — linked to proving worth through achievement
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What do you fear might happen if you fully succeed?”
“Who told you you had to earn your worth?”
“What does success mean to you — without pressure or performance?”
“What part of you still believes you’re not allowed to have it all?”
? ? Pro Tips
Mirror their brilliance back to them often — they may not see it yet
Pair with affirmations and self-worth journaling
Encourage identity work: “Who am I when I stop proving and start receiving?”
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Worthiness beliefs inventory
Redefining success worksheet
“Success is safe” visualization script
Celebration and receiving ritual builder
Coach Mindset
True success begins with self-permission.
When your client realizes they don’t have to earn, prove, or struggle to be worthy — they unlock a version of success that’s sustainable, soul-aligned, and deeply fulfilling. You’re not just helping them grow — you’re helping them receive.
Unworthiness and SUCCESS
Unworthiness Beliefs Inventory
Create a list of thoughts and behaviors that demonstrate how you have been unconsciously creating from your beliefs of unworthiness and/or failure. Here are some examples:
Thoughts Behaviors :
Nothing ever works for me I can’t do anything right.
I’ll never get that job. Nobody loves me.
I'm fat
I never have enough money. I’ll never be happy.
I have no friends.
I have nothing to do. I’m always getting sick. I’m always dating jerks.
I’m habitually late.
I misplace important items. I don’t keep appointments. I always judge my partners. I eat compulsively.
I spend excessively.
I’m always complaining.
I sit home on the couch and never call anyone. I make no effort to get involved in groups or organizations.
I don’t make the effort to eat healthy, exercise or take supplements.
I don’t ask the questions that will alert me to a person’s values
Thoughts Behaviors:
When you hear yourself thinking the thoughts on your list, or engaging in those behaviors, acknowledge yourself for noticing, forgive yourself, and create a new choice in thought and behavior that supports your new experience of success. Recognize the process of self-sabotage within you and nip it in the bud!
Celebrating Success:
Make a list of successes, triumphs and accomplishes that you have made in your life and celebrate them now!
Taking Back Your Power
Make a list of the memories you hold of parents, teachers, or anyone else who criticized you, shamed you, criticized you, embarrassed you or rejected you. For each, identify what belief about yourself that you internalized. Then, identify the ACTUAL truth.
Affirmation:
I consciously acknowledge that I am the creator of my experience. I forgive myself for perceiving circumstances through my filter of unworthiness. My creations successfully reflect my beliefs—good, bad or otherwise.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #15: Overcoming Fear of Chang e

? ? Purpose
This tool helps clients face the internal resistance that naturally arises when stepping outside their comfort zone. Whether the change is big or small, fear often masquerades as procrastination, doubt, or overwhelm. This tool helps clients acknowledge their fear, understand its roots, and move forward anyway — with clarity, self-trust, and intention.
Change becomes possible when fear no longer has the steering wheel.
When to Use It
When a client is about to take a leap (new career, relationship, identity)
When there’s hesitation, backtracking, or playing small
When emotions like anxiety, guilt, or uncertainty cloud decision-making
Anytime the client’s growth edge is visible — but they’re resisting it
How to Facilitate It
Normalize the fear. Fear doesn’t mean stop — it means pay attention. Use this tool to help clients name their resistance, disarm the fear narrative, and anchor into purpose.
Sample Script:
“Fear isn’t a sign you’re doing something wrong — it’s often a sign you’re on the right path. Let’s explore what fear is trying to protect you from, and how we can thank it without letting it run the show.”
Step-by-step process:
Identify the change the client wants to make
Uncover the fear (emotional, practical, subconscious)
Understand the protective story behind the fear
Reframe the story through truth, choice, and alignment
Create a small, safe step forward that builds courage
? ? What to Watch For
Fear disguised as logic (“I just need more time/info/money”)
Old trauma or identity patterns emerging during change
Perfectionism and people-pleasing as forms of control
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What’s the worst that could happen if you change? And what’s the best?”
“What does this fear want you to avoid or protect?”
“Is this fear coming from a past version of you — or the one you’re becoming?”
“What would it look like to take just one brave step?”
? ? Pro Tips
Use visualization (e.g., fear vs. future self dialogue)
Combine with Belief Rewiring, Indecision, or Empowered Mindset tools
Reflect on past brave moments — anchor confidence in past evidence
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Fear awareness worksheet
“Change Resistance Map” — internal dialogue, beliefs, protective instincts
Reframing section: fear to power
Courage action plan (small, aligned step with timeframe)
Coach Mindset
Fear is not the enemy — it’s a messenger.
When you help clients get curious about fear instead of avoiding it, they gain access to inner power they didn’t know they had. As their coach, you get to walk beside them as they rewrite what change means — from threat to invitation.
Overcoming Fear of Change
The following are the steps most people get STUCK in, due to fear of change.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Discontent - You grow increasingly unhappy and discontent with an area of your life. You “hang in there,” tolerate, ignore, repress, or otherwise deal with the circumstance because it is comfortable and familiar, and you fear change.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Breaking Point - Eventually your level of discontent builds high enough that you cannot take it anymore. You reach a “breaking point,” either through exhaustion or due to a dramatic event occurring that triggers the break
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Decision - You decide you’re ready to change and declare that you will no longer tolerate the undesirable situation. You take the first step toward change, giving you a short-lived sense of hope.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Fear - Usually, shortly (or immediately) after your feelings of empowerment, you encounter your fear. You become uncomfortable and anxious about the idea of changing. You doubt your decision. Both options look bleak. You feel helpless, empty.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Amnesia - The fear of change grows strong enough that it makes the original situation look much better than you originally thought. You perceive the original situation as less anxiety-producing than the change. You’re used to it; it’s comfortable; it’s familiar. Plus, it has become part of your identity, so you resist letting it go. You temporarily forget why you wanted to change it so badly.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Backtracking - Most people choose to go back to or stick with the item they wished to change. You essentially talk yourself out of changing.
There are 2 ways to break the cycle. Which do you prefer?
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Extreme Pain: You have a breaking point that is severe enough to push through the change cycle. For many people, unfortunately, it takes an extreme circumstance to push them to evolve, such as major financial loss, job loss, loss of a loved one, the ending of a relationship, a severe accident, or a nervous breakdown. You see, your Higher Self knows what you truly want and will lead you to it. If you resist changing long enough, something will happen in your life that will put you in a position where you have NO CHOICE but to change.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Self-Honesty: You have the humbling experience of realizing that there’s a part of you that doesn’t really want to change. You are comfortable with your habits, and with what you know. You have a lot of fear that holds you back. You have many self- limiting beliefs. You receive some sort of benefit from staying where you are. You are unhappy because you want to be unhappy. You are addicted to the situation. You believe your pain is you; it’s your story. You can see your resistance to letting it go. Only after reaching this level of self-honesty can you truly choose to change.
Self-Honesty Reflectio n
Can you see how this change cycle has impacted your life? (How?)
Are you ready for it to stop?
Have you experienced change amnesia before? (When?)
What will happen if you continue NOT to change?
Are you ready to swallow the pill of self-honesty, even if it is hard because you are tired of being dissatisfied?
Are you ready to take responsibility for your life and create the life you dream of having? Are you at the point where you will accept nothing less than what you truly want?
In order to be able to break the cycle, you also need to understand the underlying reasons you’ve been allowing yourself to keep avoiding change. If any of them apply to you, make a note of how you feel.
You don’t want to change.
You don’t know what you want. (Try imagining what you would want if time, money, and people did not limit you.)
Your dream isn’t big enough. (What would you do ANYTHING to attain?)
You’re letting your fear be bigger than you. (Are you really willing to settle?)
You are attached to your problem. (What would you talk about without it? Whom would you be?)
You’re benefiting from your problem. (What are you holding onto? How does it benefit you to NOT change?)

#### ? ? ️ Tool #16: Emotion Identification Char t

? ? Purpose
This tool is designed to help clients build emotional literacy — the ability to recognize, name, and understand their emotions. Many people experience emotional overwhelm, numbness, or confusion simply because they don’t have the language for what they feel.
By increasing emotional awareness, clients gain insight into their needs, patterns, and triggers — and are better equipped to make intentional choices.
When to Use It
When a client feels stuck or unable to express what they’re feeling
During conflict, overwhelm, or emotional decision-making
When exploring values, boundaries, or unmet needs
As a daily or weekly emotional check-in tool
How to Facilitate It
Introduce the chart as a mirror — not a test. Emphasize that all emotions are valid, and learning to name them is an act of self-awareness, not self-control.
Sample Script:
“You can’t manage what you don’t name. Let’s explore what’s really going on underneath the surface. Not to fix it — but to understand it.”
Walk them through:
Locate the emotion (start broad: anger, sadness, joy, fear, etc.)
Get specific using subcategories (e.g., “angry” → “frustrated,” “resentful”)
Explore the origin — what situation or thought triggered this?
Notice the body — where is this emotion felt physically?
Ask what it needs — what’s the emotion pointing to?
? ? What to Watch For
Clients who intellectualize feelings — invite them to drop into the body
Discomfort naming “negative” emotions — normalize all emotional data
Emotions layered together — tease apart primary and secondary emotions
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“Where in your body do you feel that emotion right now?”
“When was the first time you remember feeling this way?”
“What is this emotion trying to tell you or protect you from?”
“What does this feeling need in order to be heard or resolved?”
? ? Pro Tips
Recommend clients use the chart daily to check in and track trends
Pair with breathing or grounding exercises for clients who feel overwhelmed
Use in group coaching to normalize emotion-based coaching language
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Full-color emotion wheel/chart (core and secondary emotions)
Reflection prompts for each major category
Body-mapping space for somatic awareness
Journal-style prompts for deeper exploration
Coach Mindset
Emotions are data — not distractions.
By helping clients learn to name and navigate their inner world, you give them the keys to greater self-regulation, confidence, and connection. And when a client feels seen emotionally, they’re more likely to trust the coaching process — and themselves.
Emotion Identification Chart
This chart will help you get a general idea of the signs and symptoms of each emotion to make them easier to identify; specifically, easier to identify early. Keep in mind everyone experiences each emotion somewhat differently and you may not experience all of the characteristics.
LABEL EMOTION STATE BEHAVIOR
Happiness
Intense, positive feelings of wellbeing, pleasure, contentment, delight, joy, optimism, and gratitude. Affirmative, positive thoughts and mental clarity.
Head held high (posture), wideeyed, smiling, laughing, relaxation of muscles, open body language.
Pleasant voice, friendly, swinging arms, dancing.
Unhealthy Anxiety
Vague, unpleasant feelings of distress, uneasiness, stress, apprehension, and nervousness. Thoughts of uncertainty and worry, racing thoughts, difficulty concentrating and remembering.
Restlessness, sweating, clammy hands, hunched shoulders, swallowing, quickened breath, darting eyes, butterflies in the stomach, nausea.
Pacing, biting lip, fidgeting. Irritability, hypervigilance. Shutting down or withdrawing.
Healthy Anxiety (Concern)
Same emotion, but less intense.
Same physical state, but less intense.
Instead of shutting down or withdrawing, you will confront the situation and seek a solution.
Unhealthy Anger
Intense, uncomfortable feelings of hostility and hurt. Thoughts of blame and resentment. Difficulty thinking clearly or rationally.
Feeling out of control.
Muscle tension, headache, tight chest, increased heart rate, increased blood pressure, heavy breathing, clenched fist, furrowed brow, showing teeth, clenched jaw, sweating, trembling, flushed cheeks, large posture.
Loud voice, yelling, cursing, sarcasm, pacing.
Sometimes leads to aggression, including hitting a wall, throwing an object, or lashing out at a person.
Healthy Anger
Same emotion, but less intense. Feeling more in control.
Same physical state, but less intense.
While voice may be raised, behavior will be more controlled and expressive, rather than aggressive.
Unhealthy Depression
Feelings of intense pain and sorrow, guilt, unworthiness, disappointment, helplessness, gloominess, loss, grief, numbness, meaninglessness, loss of interest.
Defeated thinking and difficulty concentrating and remembering.
Slumped posture and hunched shoulders, long face, slow movements, pouting, body aches, crying, shaking, crossed arms, fatigue, upset stomach, monotone voice.
Curling up into a ball, laying around, withdrawing, irritability.
Disengaging from everyday life or enjoyable activities.
Healthy Sadness
Similar emotions but without a sense of hopelessness.
Same physical state, but less intense.
May have moments of low energy or irritability but will still engage in life and enjoyable activities.
Fear
Intense feeling of dread, impending doom, or panic due to a perceived danger or threat. Paranoid or worst- case thinking and hyper focused on the object of the fear.
Increased heart rate, increased blood pressure, alert eyes, high eyebrows, corners of cheeks pulled toward ears, clammy, sweating, quickened breath, goose bumps, butterflies in the stomach, shaky voice.
Freezing, fleeing, hiding.
Practicing Emotional Awareness and Identification
Next time you catch yourself experiencing an emotion that is distinct, ask yourself the following questions. Practice this line of questioning often, especially when experiencing unpleasant emotions.
How do I feel?
How do I know what I feel?
What sensations do I notice? Where in my body do I feel them?
Where did the feeling begin? Did it move?
How do I recognize when OTHERS experience this emotion?
Do I notice any of these signs in myself?
What do I observe in my body language, vocal tone, thoughts, and behaviors?

#### ? ? ️ Tool #17: Pain and Pleasure Principl e

? ? Purpose
This tool helps clients understand what truly motivates their behavior — the subconscious pull toward pleasure and avoidance of pain. Once a client sees how this principle is shaping their choices, you can help them rewire their associations so that change feels desirable, not daunting.
It’s a powerful mindset and behavior-shifting tool grounded in basic neuroscience and psychology.
When to Use It
When a client struggles with motivation or self-sabotage
Before setting a goal, to anchor emotional leverage
During resistance or plateau phases
Anytime behavior change or habit formation is the focus
How to Facilitate It
Introduce the principle:
“Everything we do is an attempt to avoid pain or gain pleasure. If something feels painful — even subconsciously — we’ll avoid it. Let’s uncover how this shows up for you, and shift it.”
Guide your client through the following process:
Current Behavior – What do you want to change but haven’t?
Pain Association – What negative meaning or outcome is your brain avoiding?
Pleasure Association – What are you currently gaining (even if unhelpful)?
Flip It – Link more pain to inaction, and more pleasure to taking action
Reinforcement Plan – How will you anchor this new motivation moving forward?
? ? What to Watch For
Shallow answers – go deeper into emotional pain/pleasure, not just logical outcomes
Moral judgment – help clients explore without shame or self-blame
Immediate reward trap – acknowledge the role of instant gratification vs. long-term fulfillment
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What have you linked pain to when it comes to this goal?”
“What would happen if nothing changed for the next year?”
“What’s one way this behavior is actually serving you right now?”
“How can we make the new behavior feel exciting, rewarding, or emotionally fulfilling?”
? ? Pro Tips
Ask clients to visualize the consequences of inaction over time (1 year, 5 years)
Anchor new habits to a strong “why” and emotional reward
Revisit this tool periodically — motivation evolves with identity
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Pain/Pleasure awareness map
Behavior trigger analysis
Reassociation worksheet
Motivation clarity and vision tracker
Coach Mindset
If a client isn’t changing, it’s not because they’re lazy or broken. It’s because their brain has linked more pain to the change than to staying stuck. This tool gives you the key to unlock that resistance — and help them take powerful, aligned action.
The Pain/ Pleasure Principl e
Everything we do in life is because we’re either avoiding pain or moving toward pleasure.
If you’re continuing a pattern or behavior that you don’t like, it’s because you’re linking more pain to stopping it than you are to continuing it. And if there’s something you’re not doing that you want to do, it’s because you link more pain to doing it than not doing it.
Below is an activity that will help you stop patterns and change behaviors because you associate massive pain with continuing the old pattern and you associate massive pleasure to the desired behaviors.
List 4 patterns or behaviors that you need to change in order to reach your goals/dreams and the desired new behavior or outcome:

1. Unwanted Pattern:
   Desired Outcome:
2. Unwanted Pattern:
   Desired Outcome:
3. Unwanted Pattern:
   Desired Outcome:
4. Unwanted Pattern:
   Desired Outcome:
   Now for each desired change, answer the following questions :
   PATTERN 1:
   What is the PAIN you associate with stopping the old pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you’ve gotten from doing the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PAIN that will happen if you DO NOT stop the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you will experience if you DO stop the pattern and create the desired outcome?
   PATTERN 2:
   What is the PAIN you associate with stopping the old pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you’ve gotten from doing the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PAIN that will happen if you DO NOT stop the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you will experience if you DO stop the pattern and create the desired outcome?
   PATTERN 3:
   What is the PAIN you associate with stopping the old pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you’ve gotten from doing the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PAIN that will happen if you DO NOT stop the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you will experience if you DO stop the pattern and create the desired outcome?
   PATTERN 4:
   What is the PAIN you associate with stopping the old pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you’ve gotten from doing the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PAIN that will happen if you DO NOT stop the pattern or behavior?
   What is the PLEASURE you will experience if you DO stop the pattern and create the desired outcome?

#### ? ? ️ Tool #18: Developing Awareness of Self-Tal k

? ? Purpose
This tool helps clients build conscious awareness of the internal dialogue shaping their identity, emotions, and behavior. Self-talk isn’t just mental chatter — it’s a running narrative that defines what clients believe they’re capable of.
By helping them tune in to how they speak to themselves, you create the foundation for deep mindset shifts, greater self-compassion, and authentic confidence.
When to Use It
Early in the coaching relationship to assess mindset patterns
During moments of self-doubt, anxiety, or shame
Alongside belief, habit, or identity-focused work
When a client’s actions aren’t aligning with their intentions
How to Facilitate It
Invite your client to become an observer of their thoughts rather than a judge. This tool works best when used as an ongoing practice — like journaling or voice noting — with a mix of reflection and gentle reframing.
Sample Script:
“Your inner dialogue is the background music to your life. If it’s harsh, doubtful, or critical, it will influence how you feel, decide, and show up. Let’s tune into what’s playing — and decide what kind of soundtrack you want instead.”
Step-by-step process:
Notice the self-talk in specific moments (stress, failure, achievement, etc.)
Capture it honestly — word for word, no editing
Label it — Is this fear? Doubt? Protection? Perfectionism?
Challenge and reframe into something more compassionate and empowering
Create a “power phrase” to reinforce the shift
? ? What to Watch For
Clients brushing off inner talk as “normal” — invite curiosity, not shame
Perfectionist reframes — help clients create believable, not forced, alternatives
Deep emotional roots — tie self-talk to past narratives, caregivers, or systems
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What do you say to yourself when things go wrong?”
“How would you speak to a friend in the same situation?”
“Whose voice does that inner critic sound like?”
“What’s something true and kind you could say to yourself instead?”
? ? Pro Tips
Recommend clients track their self-talk over a week — categorize common patterns
Pair with a daily journaling or affirmation habit
Use metaphor: “If your inner voice was a person, would you hang out with them?”
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Self-talk tracker worksheet
Trigger-to-thought log
Belief filter prompts (e.g., Is this true? Kind? Useful?)
Reframe and power statement builder
Coach Mindset
Self-talk isn’t just a mirror of how a client feels — it shapes how they feel. By teaching clients to upgrade their inner dialogue, you’re giving them the tools to become their own coach, cheerleader, and grounded guide — long after your sessions end.
Developing Awareness of Self-Tal k
Negative Self-Talk Triggers

1. Self-Limiting. What do you hear your inner critic say that sounds like an excuse?
   Why does it say you can’t do what you want?
   What does it say when it is shutting down possibilities?
2. Assumptions. What does your inner critic tend to assume about?
   When does it tend to think it can read people’s minds?
   What does it tend to assume other people will think about you?
   What stories does it tell you that probably aren’t even true?
3. Re-runs. What repetitive, automatic thoughts have you been thinking for a long time?
   What memories do you tend to replay in your mind over and over again?
   What stories from your past or about yourself do you tend to talk about?
   What phrases do you say to yourself or others repeatedly (especially the ones when you’re judging yourself)? For example: “I’m always late” or “I’m an idiot” or “here we go again” or “this always happens to me”.
4. Others’ Thoughts. Who’s voice to you regularly hear in your head?
   What do they say?
   What do you tell yourself you “should” do?
   Do you really believe that you “should” do this? (Hint, if you’re feeling a sense of guilt, it’s probably not your own, ori ginal, belief.)
5. If yes, make it a MUST and do it.
6. If not—if this is someone else hijacking your mind, tell them to GET OUT and then ask yourself, what do I really believe?
   What’s Your Inner Critic’s Personality
   The worrier: Points out everything that can go wrong. Stirs up emotions of anxiety and fear by imagining disasters, expecting the worst, and overestimating the odds of something bad happening. It tends to say “what if”?
   The critic: Constantly judges and evaluates your behavior and points out your flaws. Jumps on any mistake you make and reminds you of past failures. Compares you to others and assumes they will judge you. It even minimizes your accomplishments! It tends to say “you’re an idiot”.
   The victim: It tells you that you’re hopeless, not making progress, or that it’s too hard. It tells you there is something wrong with you, your incapable, unworthy. You’re not smart enough. There are too many obstacles in your way. It’s not your fault. It tends to say “I can’t”.
   The perfectionist: It pushes you to do better but even when you do better you still feel like you’re not good enough. There is always more you should be doing. Mistakes and setbacks must be avoided or quickly moved past. It pushes you to seek external validation, achievement, status. Acceptance by others is of the utmost importance. It probably even stops you from taking action because you’re afraid to fail. Tends to say “I need to do better” or “I’m not good enough”.
   Take Your Power Back from Bob
   Now that you know what to look out for so you can notice your inner critic in action, go out into the world and practice observing it. When you catch your Bob in the act, use the following 3 strategies to take your power back from these negative thoughts.
   IGNORE BOB: Don’t take BOB seriously. When BOB starts rambling on incessantly or hops on a negative train, imagine BOB has a funny voice or is wearing a clown suit. BOB is not you, and it doesn’t know what it’s talking about.
   PROTECT BOB: BOB’s easily influenced, so always ask yourself if YOU really believe what it’s saying. We already talked about getting people out of your head. One way to do this is pay special attention for any thoughts coming from BOB that sound eerily similar to things other people say (such as your parents, the media, authority figures). Choose what you expose BOB to wisely, because he’s apt to believe it and repeat it.
   OBSERVE BOB: As often as you can, remind yourself to watch your BOB. Notice what it’s thinking about. If you don’t like what it’s thinking about, CHOOSE A NEW THOUGHT. You’re in charge. Many of the activities discussed throughout this course are designed to help you observe, record, and re-direct your bob.
   Remember that it takes time to get good at keeping your BOB in check. You’ll notice times when BOB runs off on a tangent of terrible thoughts without you noticing—sneaky BOB! But no worries because when you eventually notice what BOB is doing you can WHACK BOB on the head—it’s like playing Whack-a-Mole.
   Whack him and say “bad bob!” and laugh.
   This stops the negative thought, giving you a moment to remember that you have a choice. You can then implement one of the thought-changing strategies you learn in the course and pick a better thought. The more you observe your BOB the better you’ll get at catching it in the act— and as you practice, the voice will get quieter and your inner cheerleader will take the lead.
   Play whack-a mole with your inner critic!

### Section 4: Decision-Making & Taking Action

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
M ove clients from stuck to self-led—with clarity, commitment, and follow-through.
As a coach, you’re not just helping clients “get things done.”
You’re helping them become someone who follows through—even when it’s hard, unclear, or scary.
This section is about bridging the gap between insight and action.
Because awareness is important, but without execution, transformation stalls.
Clients often come to coaching with big goals but find themselves stuck in:
Overthinking or decision paralysis
Fear of failure, judgment, or making the “wrong” choice
A lifetime of unmet goals and broken self-trust
As a coach, your role isn’t to force action. It’s to:
Help clients uncover what’s really holding them back
Guide them to make aligned, confident decisions
Create simple, repeatable frameworks for consistent progress
The tools in this section give you the structure to do just that.
They’re designed to help clients build internal motivation, external accountability, and the habits that turn action into identity.
Because when a client consistently takes aligned action, they don’t just reach goals—they become unstoppable.
This section helps you coach them there.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #19: Overcoming Indecision and Inacti on

? ? Purpose
This tool is for clients who are stuck in mental loops — second-guessing, overanalyzing, or waiting for the “perfect” time to act. It helps them clarify decisions, trust their inner guidance, and move forward even when they’re unsure.
Because clarity often comes after action — not before it.
When to Use It
When a client feels paralyzed by too many options
When fear of making the “wrong” choice is blocking progress
During major life transitions, business shifts, or goal planning
Anytime indecision is draining motivation or momentum
How to Facilitate It
Use this tool to normalize indecision while guiding the client to choose movement over perfection. Focus on helping them understand what’s really driving their hesitation.
Sample Script:
“It’s okay not to feel 100% sure. But let’s get curious about what’s keeping you frozen — and what would feel like a low-risk, high-trust next step.”
Guide them through:
Name the decision and the stuck point
Identify fears, risks, or emotional blocks
Clarify values and priorities tied to the decision
Explore best-case and worst-case scenarios
Choose one next aligned action
? ? What to Watch For
Fear-based questions – help reframe from “What if it goes wrong?” to “What if it works?”
Binary thinking – open up the space between yes/no or right/wrong
Need for external validation – shift focus inward toward values and intuition
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What’s the cost of not deciding?”
“What would ‘good enough’ look like instead of perfect?”
“If you fully trusted yourself, what would you choose?”
“What’s the smallest next step you can take to test this path?”
? ? Pro Tips
Encourage clients to try a direction before committing — clarity grows with action
Use visualization or journaling to explore emotional truths under indecision
Support follow-up accountability after the decision is made to reinforce momentum
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Decision clarity worksheet
Fear-vs-values assessment
Scenario mapping (best/worst outcomes)
Action commitment and reflection log
Coach Mindset
Most clients aren’t afraid of failing — they’re afraid of regret. Help them see that indecision is a decision, too — one that often costs more than choosing and adjusting. Your job isn’t to give them the answer. It’s to help them access the courage to move.
Overcoming Indecisio n
Are you on autopilot?
What have you chosen to do because it was what you were “supposed” to do?
What did you really want to do that you didn’t allow yourself to do?
What do you choose to do by default (like watching TV or being on social media)?
What else could you be choosing to do instead?
What do you actually WANT to do with your life?
Not Knowing What You Want:
In what areas of your life are you not sure what you want?
In what areas of your life do you get stuck at a decision point and just think, think, think?
Have you ever missed out on an opportunity because you didn’t make a decision in time?
What decisions are you read to make now so that you do not miss the opportunity to choose?
Perfectionism:
What decisions have you struggled to make because you’re waiting for it to be perfect?
What decisions have you held yourself back from because you’re afraid of making the wrong decision?
What decisions are you ready to make now, accepting that the worst decision is not to move forward?
Being Indecisive:
Are you not sure which option to choose?
In what way could you try or test each option?
If you can’t actually try it out, run through the possibilities in your mind.\*
Ask yourself, what are the possible outcomes?
How do I feel about each outcome?
For each outcome, what are the possible next steps?
After considering these options, what feels like the best choice for you?
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Feeling Uncertain:
In what ways are you avoiding making a decision to move forward because you’re not sure how it will turn out?
Is there a way you could try it out or find out more?
If not, simply do it! You may never be able to predict the outcome.
If you cannot get yourself to take action, see the Overcoming Inaction video.
If fear is holding you back, see the Fear Setting video.
What decisions are you ready to make, even if you cannot know the outcome, knowing that you do not want to continue to put this off?
Are you facing any life-changing decisions or irrevocable choices?
What choice are you facing?
What is option #1?
What is option #2?
For each option, the result will lead to a different life with the following activity. Imagine you are choosing to live LIFE #1 and allowing LIFE #2 to drift out to sea.
What are the positive, meaningful outcomes I’ll experience if I choose LIFE #1?
What are the negative, meaningful losses I’ll experience because I did NOT choose LIFE #2?
Now, switch your choice around in your mind, allowing LIFE #1 to drift to sea, and imagine what it would be like.
What are the positive, meaningful outcomes I’ll experience if I choose LIFE #2?
What are the negative, meaningful losses I’ll experience because I do NOT choose LIFE #1?
When you’re 85 years old, which one would you regret NOT doing more?
After doing this exercise, which option feels like it is best for you?
What can you do to honor, accept, and release the other option, to be at peace with letting it board your ghost ship and sail away

#### ? ? ️ Tool #20: Eliminating Excuse s

? ? Purpose
This tool is designed to help clients uncover and dismantle the excuses that are keeping them stuck. Excuses aren’t just obstacles — they’re often protective mechanisms rooted in fear, perfectionism, or self-doubt. This tool brings those patterns to the surface and transforms them into empowered choices.
By helping your client take ownership without shame, you create space for aligned, courageous action.
When to Use It
When a client consistently avoids taking action
During goal-setting or progress review sessions
When self-sabotage, procrastination, or indecision show up
To break through mental resistance or victim mindset
How to Facilitate It
Begin with compassion, not confrontation. This is not about “calling the client out” — it’s about lovingly holding up a mirror so they can see where they’re blocking their own success.
Sample Script:
“We all have stories we tell ourselves to stay safe. Let’s explore what’s been getting in the way of your progress — and decide what you’re ready to let go of.”
Walk them through:
Identify a stuck area or goal they’re avoiding
Name the excuse(s) they use — time, money, energy, fear, etc.
Explore what the excuse protects them from
Challenge the excuse’s truth or usefulness
Create a new belief and aligned action
? ? What to Watch For
Excuses disguised as logic (e.g., “It’s just not the right time”) — gently challenge assumptions
Self-judgment — reframe this work as empowerment, not blame
Deep emotional roots — be ready to pair with inner child, fear of failure, or belief work
? ? ️ Coaching Prompts
“What’s the story you’ve been telling yourself about why this isn’t possible?”
“What’s the real fear underneath that story?”
“If this excuse didn’t exist, what would be possible?”
“What’s one brave step you can take, even if the excuse still feels real?”
? ? Pro Tips
Use this tool in tandem with Rewiring Limiting Beliefs or Pain/Pleasure Principle
Invite your client to rewrite their top 3 most common excuses
Turn “I can’t because…” into “I can if…” to shift into creative problem-solving
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Common excuses list with self-assessment prompts
“Excuse to Empowerment” belief flip worksheet
Ownership and action tracker
Coaching journal space for reflection and breakthroughs
Coach Mindset
Excuses are never random — they’re clues. When a client understands the need behind the excuse, they can meet it in a healthier way. Your job is to be curious, not critical — and to hold space for the moment they finally say:
“I’m done playing small.”
Eliminate Excuses (Say "No" to "But" )
So, you have tools for success, you have made a decision to create your life, you’re willing to grow as you go along, and you’re ready to take action. But, your unconscious, limiting beliefs— your excuses—could still hold you back if you don’t nip them in the bud.
Say “no” to “BUT”! BUT is the word that usually precedes an excuse. The dictionary defines an excuse as: “self-justification; 'a defense of some offensive behavior or some failure to keep a promise'.” “Buts” are simply what you use to self-justify why you are not living the life you truly desire. Below are common “buts” that many of us use. If you are honest with yourself, you will see that these are in fact excuses and not legitimate reasons. The question is, then, why do we use these “buts?” Each “but” serves its own purpose, but ultimately they all help us to remain safe— to stay where we’re comfortable.
But, it’s too hard. Is it really too hard? How would you know; have you done it? You have made it through so-called “hard” things before, haven’t you? Saying “but” gives the illusion that what you want is not possible so that you can avoid doing it.
But, it’s too risky. An intelligent decision based on a deep desire, good research, and a solid plan is not risky at all. You choose to fear risk instead of facing your other fears, like failure.
But, it’ll take too long. What is a “long time” anyway? For that matter, what is “time?” It is more accurate to look at time as an emotion, not a unit of measure. How “long” something takes has nothing to do with how much clock time passes and everything to do with how you feel. So, then why does it feel like it will take so “long?” Because you feel overwhelmed! In reality, time will pass anyway, regardless of whether or not you make the change. You say this as a way to put off making a decision. Really, you fear commitment, not time.
But, it’s overwhelming. If you are feeling overwhelmed it’s because you are thinking too big. It’s important to see the big picture, but you don’t want to “bite off more than you can chew.” Break it down into manageable chunks and stay focused on the positive.
But, I don’t have time. This is the most commonly used “but,” and it is totally bogus. In “It’ll take too long” we discussed how time is simply an emotion. So, by saying you “don’t have time” you’re saying you feel overextended or inefficient. You may not want to admit it, but you have chosen your life situations. If you are overextended it was your choice. It's a great reason not to take action. We all make time for what is important to us.
There are three solutions that can help you “make the time.”
Organize your life to free up time
Eliminate lesser important activities
Change your perspective
We are all guilty of using “buts,” and we all suffer the consequences—not living the life we really want. Use the worksheet t o assess what “buts” are holding you back.
WORKSHEET: Excuses… Say NO to But!
Which of the following common “buts” has held you back in the past?

#### ? ? ️ Tool #21: Decision-Making Framework

Empower clients to make clear, aligned choices—even in uncertainty.
? ? Purpose
This tool helps clients develop a conscious, repeatable process for making decisions—especially when they feel overwhelmed, stuck in overthinking, or afraid of making the “wrong” choice.
Many clients struggle with decisions not because they don’t know what to do—but because they don’t trust themselves to choose.
This framework helps them move from anxiety or indecision into clarity, values-based alignment, and self-trust.
When to Use It
When a client is stuck between two or more options
When fear, overthinking, or people-pleasing is blocking action
When a decision feels high-stakes or emotionally charged
As a practice tool for building internal decision-making confidence
How to Facilitate It
Introduce the process as a decision clarity map—a way to zoom out, sort emotions from logic, and reconnect with the client’s deeper truth.
Walk them through this 6-step process:
Name the Decision
“What choice are you facing right now?”
Clarify the Stakes
“What’s important about this decision? What are you afraid of?”
Check for Alignment
“Which option is most aligned with your values, vision, or long-term goals?”
Consult Head & Heart
“What does your logic say?”
“What does your intuition/body say?”
Future-Project Each Option
“Imagine you made this choice. How would you feel one week, one month, one year from now?”
Decide and Declare
“What decision are you ready to commit to—and what’s one small step you’ll take this week?”
? ? ️ Sample Script
“Let’s step outside the stress of ‘what if’ and get grounded in what matters. You’re not here to make the perfect choice—you’re here to make the aligned one. Let’s find the one that supports your future self and moves you forward.”
? ? What to Watch For
Clients trying to get it “right” instead of aligned
Obsessing over what others might think
Avoidance disguised as indecision
Nervous system dysregulation (you may need to regulate before facilitating logic)
? ? Coach Prompts
“If you trusted yourself completely, what would you do?”
“Which option feels heavier? Which feels more free?”
“What values are being honored—or violated—by each choice?”
“Are you trying to avoid regret or choose growth?”
? ? What’s Inside the Template
Decision Clarity Worksheet
Values Alignment Checklist
Logic vs. Intuition Table
Future Visualization Prompts
One-Page Decision Commitment Form
? ? Coach Mindset
Your client isn’t just choosing a path—they’re practicing self-leadership.
The goal isn’t to eliminate all doubt. It’s to teach clients to move forward with it. When you help them make empowered, values-aligned decisions—even imperfect ones—you’re building identity-level trust that will serve them far beyond this moment.
? ? Decision-Making Fra mework Template
Step 1: Name the Decision
What choice are you currently facing?
✍ ️ Write your decision or the options you’re weighing.
? ? Step 2: Clarify the Stakes
Why does this decision feel important or difficult?
What’s at stake for you?
What are you afraid might happen (if you get it wrong)?
✍ ️ Reflect on emotions, fears, or perceived consequences.
? ? Step 3: Check for Alignment
Which option is most aligned with your values and long-term goals?
Use this checklist to evaluate each option:
Option Aligned with my values? Supports my long-term vision? Feels like growth? Option A: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ☐ Yes / ☐ No ☐ Yes / ☐ No ☐ Yes / ☐ No Option B: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ☐ Yes / ☐ No ☐ Yes / ☐ No ☐ Yes / ☐ No
✍ ️ Note any conflicts or surprising insights.
Step 4: Consult Head & Heart
What does each part of you say?
Inner Voice What does it say about this decision? Logic E.g., “This makes financial sense…” Intuition E.g., “Something about this doesn’t feel right…”
✍ ️ Do the two agree or conflict? What stands out?
? ? Step 5: Future Projection

Visualize yourself having made each choice:
In 1 week:
In 1 month:
In 1 year:

How did this process feel?
How can you repeat this next time you’re stuck?

#### ? ? ️ Tool #22: Habit Tracker & Daily Action Planner

Build consistency. Bridge the gap between vision and execution.
? ? Purpose
While breakthroughs in coaching often happen during sessions, transformation occurs between them. This tool is designed to help your client turn insights into habits and stay accountable to their goals through consistent, aligned daily action.
The Habit Tracker builds awareness and motivation, while the Daily Action Planner promotes structure, prioritization, and intentional living. Together, they turn inspiration into momentum.
When to Use It
When a client is ready to build new routines or behaviors
When follow-through or time management is a struggle
To support integration of other coaching tools (mindset, goals, etc.)
When clients want to measure progress and celebrate wins
How to Facilitate It
Choose 1–3 habits that support their current coaching focus
(e.g., meditation, daily outreach, journaling, exercise)
Introduce the weekly habit tracking system as a way to build self-trust
Use the Daily Action Planner to align each day’s priorities with long-term goals
Review the tracker/planner weekly to celebrate wins and adjust strategy
? ? Frame it as a commitment to the future self—not perfection, but progress.
? ? ️ Sample Script
“This is where your growth becomes your lifestyle. Let’s build rhythm around the actions that move you forward, and celebrate each small win along the way.”
? ? What to Watch For
Clients setting too many habits or overfilling their daily to-do’s
Perfectionism and guilt around “missed” checkmarks
A lack of clarity around why each habit matters
Using the planner as a punishment vs. a support system
? ? Coach Mindset
Habits are not about discipline alone—they’re identity practices.
By supporting your client in making small daily promises—and keeping them—you’re helping them become someone who follows through. This tool cultivates structure with heart.

### ✅ Section 5: Values & Identity Wor k

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
A ligning with truth. Becoming who you’re meant to be.
As coaches, we often focus on helping clients set goals, shift mindsets, and take action—but without clarity around who they are at their core, these strategies only go so far.
This section invites your client into one of the most powerful layers of transformation: identity alignment. It’s where real, lasting change happens—not because someone is forcing themselves to act differently, but because they see themselves differently.
When a client discovers their core values, they gain a compass.
When they rewrite outdated identity scripts, they regain power.
When they define success on their terms, they stop chasing someone else’s life.
? ? As a coach, here’s what you need to know:
Most clients have never consciously defined their values—they’re operating on inherited or reactive belief systems.
Many clients’ identities are shaped by past roles, trauma, or approval-seeking—not their highest truth.
Without identity work, clients may experience success but still feel empty, confused, or misaligned.
Your job is not to give them their values—it’s to help them reveal what’s already there.
This section helps you guide clients to:
Clarify their non-negotiable values—the core principles they want to live by
Reclaim their authentic identity beyond roles, labels, or expectations
Define what success and fulfillment look like for them, not society
Make aligned decisions and take action rooted in who they truly are
Even one breakthrough here can create a ripple effect across every area of your client’s life—work, relationships, health, and purpose.
This is the work that helps clients stop chasing and start becoming.
And when a coach knows how to hold space for that?
That’s when lives change—deeply and permanently.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #23: Values Clarification Exercis e

Define your client’s compass. Empower decision-making with clarity and conviction.
? ? Purpose
Our values shape every choice we make—whether we’re conscious of them or not. This tool helps your client bring their core values into conscious awareness, so they can make decisions that feel aligned, navigate challenges with clarity, and build a life that reflects who they truly are.
When clients are unclear on their values, they often experience inner conflict, burnout, or regret. When they are clear, they gain confidence, peace of mind, and a deeper sense of purpose.
When to Use It
Early in the coaching relationship to lay a strong foundation
When a client is facing a tough decision or feeling stuck
During career, relationship, or life transitions
When there’s a mismatch between external success and internal fulfillment
How to Facilitate It
Frame the purpose: Let your client know that values are their personal GPS—guiding their choices, priorities, and sense of fulfillment.
Explore core values: Use the worksheet (below) to identify which values most resonate and why.
Narrow it down: Help your client select their top 5 core values.
Clarify meaning: For each value, ask them to define what it means to them, and how it looks in action.
Reflect on alignment: Prompt your client to evaluate how aligned their current life is with these values.
? ? ️ Sample Coaching Prompts
“When you think about times you felt proud, fulfilled, or fully alive—what values were you living out?”
“What value do you find yourself violating most often? What’s the cost?”
“Which value are you craving more of right now—and what would it look like to honor it?”
⚠ ️ What to Watch For
Clients choosing values based on what they “should” value vs. what they deeply feel
Generic or vague language (“success,” “kindness”) without personal meaning
A gap between chosen values and current behavior—use this to identify growth opportunities
Clients who resist the exercise—invite curiosity, not perfection

#### ? ? ️ Tool #24: Who Am I ?

Support your client in rewriting their identity from the inside out.
? ? Purpose
Most people go through life operating from an identity they didn’t consciously choose. It’s shaped by roles, labels, cultural conditioning, past pain, or other people’s expectations. This tool helps your client step back and ask the most powerful question in personal growth:
“Who am I—really?”
By exploring identity beyond surface-level traits, clients can reconnect with their authentic self and consciously craft the identity they want to lead with. This tool is a powerful companion to values work and a crucial step before setting goals or taking action.
When to Use It
When a client feels lost, stuck, or disconnected
During major transitions (career, relationships, life stage)
When working through imposter syndrome or low self-worth
As a bridge between values work and vision-setting
How to Facilitate It
Create safety: Let your client know this is deep work—not about fixing, but uncovering.
Explore past roles: Have them list the labels or identities they’ve taken on (e.g., mother, achiever, people pleaser).
Release what no longer fits: Invite them to identify which parts feel outdated, inauthentic, or externally imposed.
Craft a new identity: Prompt them to define who they choose to be now—based on truth, not fear or approval.
Integrate: Ask how they can start showing up from this new identity daily.
? ? ️ Powerful Coaching Prompts
“What identities have you outgrown—but still cling to?”
“Who are you when no one’s watching?”
“What parts of yourself have you hidden to be accepted?”
“If you fully trusted yourself, who would you be? ”
“Who are you becoming?”
⚠ ️ What to Watch For
Clients defaulting to resume-style answers or roles
Fear-based identities (“I’m a fighter,” “I’m broken,” “I’m a perfectionist”)
Resistance—normalize it, this work can feel vulnerable
Opportunities to affirm the client’s authentic qualities they may downplay
? ? Coach Mindset
Helping your client answer “Who am I?” isn’t about arriving at a fixed label—it’s about reconnecting them to their essence. When they start living from that place, everything else—decisions, boundaries, relationships—begins to align naturally.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #25: Defining Personal Success

Help your client redefine success based on their truth—not external exp ectations.
? ? Purpose
So many clients set goals based on what they’ve been told success should look like—money, titles, approval, or busyness. But true fulfillment only comes when success is defined from within. This tool helps your client step back from society’s standards and reconnect with what success really means to them.
It empowers them to live intentionally, measure progress by their own values, and let go of comparison or pressure to conform.
When to Use It
At the beginning of a coaching engagement
During goal-setting or mid-program reflection
When a client feels stuck despite external achievements
If they’re experiencing burnout, self-doubt, or comparison
How to Facilitate It
Normalize the redefinition: Let your client know it’s common to chase goals that don’t lead to fulfillment.
Deconstruct borrowed definitions: Explore what they’ve been taught success means (e.g., from family, school, media).
Surface authentic values: Guide them to identify what actually brings them a sense of meaning, energy, and purpose.
Create a personal definition: Help them craft a “success statement” that reflects their current season and values.
Align goals: Revisit their current goals to make sure they reflect this redefined version.
? ? ️ Powerful Coaching Prompts
“Whose version of success are you currently living?”
“When in your life did you feel most successful—and why?”
“If you weren’t trying to prove anything, what would success look like?”
“What does a successful day look like—not just a successful life?”
“If you already felt successful, how would you live differently?”
⚠ ️ What to Watch For
Clients mistaking achievement for fulfillment
Language that reflects societal pressure instead of intrinsic desire
Guilt or fear around redefining success (e.g., “Am I allowed to want that?”)
Disconnection between their goals and values—use this tool to realign
Coach Mindset
Helping clients redefine success is one of the most liberating breakthroughs you can offer. When they finally let go of what they “should” want, and start building a life around what truly matters, that’s when real transformation begins.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #26: Coaching Session Prep For m

Empower your clients to show up clear, focused, and ready to grow.
? ? Purpose
This simple form helps clients prepare mentally and emotionally for each coaching session. It encourages reflection, accountability, and intentional focus—maximizing the value of every session. It also helps the coach quickly assess patterns, priorities, and where the client most needs support.
When to Use It
Send to clients 24–48 hours before each coaching session
Use during the session to guide your flow
Encourage self-reflection in between sessions for deeper insights
How to Facilitate It
You can send this form digitally via email or as a Google Form, or use it as a printable worksheet. Let clients know that preparing for sessions isn’t about perfection—it’s about presence and progress.
Coach Mindset Tip
A prepared client is an empowered client. When clients take a few minutes to reflect before a session, the conversation often becomes richer, more focused, and more productive. Consider creating a reusable digital form or email reminder for this to make it a habit.
Coaching Session Prep Form Template

#### ? ? ️ Tool #27: Client Progress Tracke r

Support lasting change by tracking wins, patterns, and milestones over time.
? ? Purpose
Lasting transformation happens through consistent, aligned action over time. This tool empowers both coach and client to monitor growth, recognize patterns, and stay accountable to meaningful progress—not just busywork. It also helps the coach adjust strategies based on real data and client insights.
When to Use It
At the end of each session to summarize action steps
Monthly or quarterly to reflect on broader progress
During reviews, milestone check-ins, or program transitions
How to Facilitate It
You can use this tool as:
A physical tracker in printed workbooks
A digital spreadsheet or fillable PDF
A shared document for collaborative tracking
Encourage clients to take ownership by updating it regularly. Review together at least once a month.

#### ? ? ️ Tool #30: Powerful Coaching Questions Cheat Sheet

Elevate your sessions by asking the right question s at the right time.
? ? Purpose
Great coaching isn’t about giving the right answers—it’s about asking the right questions. This cheat sheet gives coaches a curated list of powerful, open-ended prompts that drive reflection, unlock clarity, and lead to transformation.
These questions are grouped by category so you can quickly find what fits your client’s moment—whether they need breakthrough, focus, or forward movement.
How to Use It
Reference during sessions when you feel stuck or want to go deeper
Use as inspiration when creating worksheets or coaching programs
Share a few prompts with clients as journaling reflections between sessions
? ? Coach Mindset
These questions are tools for transformation—but your presence is what makes them powerful. Use them with curiosity, compassion, and the courage to hold space for whatever arises.
? ? ️ 30 Powerful Coaching Questions
? ? Self-Awareness & Identity
Who are you when you’re not trying to be who others expect you to be?
What do you believe about yourself that may no longer be true?
What parts of yourself have you been hiding—and why?
If you fully trusted yourself, how would you show up differently?
What do you want to be known for?
? ? Values & Alignment
What truly matters most to you right now?
What would feel like success on your terms?
What values are being honored—or violated—in your current situation?
Where in your life are you settling for “fine” instead of aligned?
If you said no to what no longer fits, what could you say yes to?
? ? Vision & Purpose
What does your ideal future look like—and why does it matter?
If nothing were off limits, what would you create or pursue?
What would you do if you knew you could not fail?
Who do you need to become to live the life you want?
What impact do you feel called to make?
? ? Clarity & Decision-Making
What decision have you been avoiding—and what’s the cost?
What does your head say? What does your heart say?
If you trusted your future self, what would they tell you to do?
What’s one step you can take, even if you don’t have it all figured out?
What would choosing growth look like in this moment?
? ? Mindset & Emotional Mastery
What story are you telling yourself—and is it empowering or limiting?
What emotion are you avoiding feeling—and why?
What’s one belief you’re ready to release?
What would it look like to lead with courage instead of fear?
How do you want to feel—and what’s in your control to create that?
? ? Integration & Action
What’s one small promise you can make—and keep—to yourself this week?
What would progress (not perfection) look like right now?
What needs to happen next to move this forward?
What support do you need—and are you willing to ask for it?
What’s the one thing you’ll look back on and be proud you did?
